title: VIDEO PLATFORM (YOUTUBE)
subtitle: Two hard problems: getting gigabyte uploads in reliably, and streaming smoothly on any connection.
footer: DDIA: Ch 10 batch DAGs · Ch 1 bandwidth math   ·   Similar: File storage and sync · Photo sharing

items: Upload directly to object storage with presigned, multipart, resumable URLs; bytes never touch your servers.
Split videos into segments and transcode them in parallel into several resolutions.
Serve segments from a CDN and let the player switch quality per segment (adaptive bitrate).
Upload videos (up to many GB)
Watch videos with smooth playback on any network
Resumable uploads
Fast start, adaptive quality
~1M uploads/day; billions of views
Metadata availability over consistency
1M uploads/day × 1GB raw ≈ 1PB/day raw, plus several renditions.
Views are mostly served from the CDN, not origin.

blocks.text: Naive: upload gigabytes through your API servers. Slow, fragile, and expensive.

items: The API returns presigned multipart URLs; the client uploads parts directly to S3 in parallel and resumes failed parts.
An S3 event starts a transcoding DAG: split into short segments, transcode each to several resolutions in parallel, write HLS/DASH manifests, and mark the video READY.
Viewers fetch the manifest and segments from the CDN; the player picks the quality per segment from measured bandwidth (adaptive bitrate).
Why presigned URLs?
Bytes never touch your servers; S3 handles scale; multipart gives parallel, resumable parts.
Fast transcoding?
Segment-level parallelism across many workers; the DAG orchestrator tracks completion.
Adaptive bitrate?
The manifest lists renditions; the player switches per segment.
Cost?
Transcode popular formats eagerly; long-tail renditions lazily.
Serving or uploading whole files through app servers.
Adding parts before a number shows they are needed.
Ignoring retries, timeouts and crashes.
